drip.author: vinyl_endgame
drip.title: Records that only make sense once the evenings start getting dark early
drip.body:
There's a week every September when I stop reaching for anything bright and start pulling out the quiet records. Pink Moon always goes on first. Under half an hour, almost nothing but Nick Drake and a guitar, and it sounds like a room with one lamp on.

After that it's usually Astral Weeks, then Either/Or. What's in your early-dark rotation?

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: Pink Moon is the right call, but everyone reaches for the title track. the real ones are Road and Things Behind the Sun. the whole record is quiet and the deep cuts are the ones that actually sound like October.

replies.author: vinyl_endgame
replies.body: Things Behind the Sun at dusk with the window cracked open is the entire reason I own a turntable.

comments.author: SixStringBudget
comments.body: For Emma, Forever Ago. The story is it was recorded in a cabin over a winter, and you can hear the cold in it. Also every guitarist I know tried to learn Skinny Love, and every guitarist I know gave up at the tuning.

comments.author: reversecowbell
comments.body: Mine's less folk: Disintegration by The Cure. Not sad-quiet, sad-huge. Rain on the window, headphones on, and Plainsong taking its sweet time to arrive.

comments.author: quietkettle
comments.body: I don't own a turntable, but a friend once made me a playlist called 'kettle weather' and it was mostly Joni Mitchell's Blue. I've played it every autumn since, and the tea goes cold every single time.

replies.author: vinyl_endgame
replies.body: 'kettle weather' is the best name for a season I've ever heard. Blue on a grey afternoon is exactly right. letting the tea go cold is part of the ritual.

drip.author: SixStringBudget
drip.title: Six weeks with a metronome and I've learned that I rush every single chorus
drip.body:
Update from the lessons front. My teacher set a metronome on the music stand and asked me to play a song I've known for fifteen years. I have never been so humbled by a clicking noise.

Verses: fine. Chorus: I speed up like I'm late for a bus. Every time. He says it's the most common thing he hears from self-taught players, because we all learned by playing along to the exciting part of the record.

It's getting better. Slowly. At exactly the tempo I set, which is the whole problem.

comments.author: reversecowbell
comments.body: Record yourself without the click, then play it back against one. Did that once in the band days and discovered our 'mid-tempo ballad' was actually two songs at different speeds glued together at the bridge.

replies.author: SixStringBudget
replies.body: two songs glued at the bridge is how my version of anything sounds. recording myself sounds terrifying, which means it's probably necessary

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: slight defence of the rush: plenty of great records speed up. bands used to track live with no click, and the chorus lifted because the room got excited. a perfectly gridded chorus can be a chorus with no pulse.

replies.author: SixStringBudget
replies.body: I'm going to show this to my teacher and he's going to say 'learn the rule before you break it' and he's going to be right

comments.author: half_marathon_harold
comments.body: Runners call this going out too fast. The first kilometre feels like the chorus and you pay for it at the end. Start slower than feels right and finish strong. Works on legs, probably works on hands.

drip.author: b_side_believer
drip.title: The best covers rescue songs that were never hits in the first place
drip.body:
Everyone's great-covers list is the same famous songs made slightly more famous. fine. but my favourite thing a cover can do is take a deep cut nobody heard and hand it to the world.

Hallelujah is the obvious one. Leonard Cohen's original was an album track that didn't go far at first, and it took other people's versions, John Cale's and then Jeff Buckley's, for it to become the song everyone knows. Song to the Siren is another: This Mortal Coil found it on a Tim Buckley record and made it haunting.

who else got rescued?

comments.author: reversecowbell
comments.body: Nothing Compares 2 U. Prince wrote it for The Family, a side project most people never heard, and then Sinéad O'Connor's version went everywhere.

replies.author: b_side_believer
replies.body: perfect example, because the original isn't bad, it was just in the wrong room. sometimes a cover is a change of address.

comments.author: vinyl_endgame
comments.body: Pushback: sometimes the rescue flattens it. Hallelujah got covered so often it turned into a montage song, and a lot of the strangeness in Cohen's verses got left on the floor. I'm glad people know it. I'm not sure they know it.

replies.author: b_side_believer
replies.body: fair, but the strange verses are still sitting there for anyone who goes looking. that's the deal with deep cuts. the door stays open.

comments.author: SixStringBudget
comments.body: Guitarist pick: Hendrix doing All Along the Watchtower. Not a rescue exactly, but Dylan's original is a short acoustic song with harmonica and Hendrix heard an entire storm in it. Even Dylan's own live versions ended up leaning toward that arrangement.

drip.author: reversecowbell
drip.title: Tell me about the smallest show you've ever been to. Either side of the stage counts
drip.body:
I'll go first. My band once played a Tuesday in a bar where the audience was the bartender, a guy waiting on his takeout, and our sound tech, who left during the second song to move his car.

We played the whole set anyway. The takeout guy clapped after every song and stayed for one extra. I think about him more than any crowd we ever had.

Tiny shows are the best shows. Prove me right.

comments.author: vinyl_endgame
comments.body: A folk singer in a used record shop, maybe twelve of us sitting on crates between the bins. No PA, no mic. When she stopped singing you could hear the fridge humming in the back room. Best show I've ever seen, and I bought her record off the counter afterward.

replies.author: reversecowbell
replies.body: buying the record off the counter is the highest honour a tiny show can get. rent money and a memory in one transaction.

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: went to see a headliner once and left in love with the opener, who played to maybe fifteen people while the bar talked over them. the headliner was fine. the opener's record is still in my rotation. the real show is always the one before the one you paid for.

comments.author: SixStringBudget
comments.body: From the other side: my first open mic, the whole room was three people waiting for their turn plus my wife. One of the three gave me a little nod when I finished. I lived on that nod for a month.

replies.author: reversecowbell
replies.body: a nod from another nervous musician beats a standing ovation. that person knew exactly what it cost you to get up there.

drip.author: vinyl_endgame
drip.title: Liner notes sent me down a hole: the same few session players are on half my favourite records
drip.body:
It started with the credits on the back of a reissue and turned into a rabbit hole. A lot of the sixties records I love share the same hands. The Wrecking Crew in LA, the Funk Brothers at Motown. Most of them weren't even credited on the original sleeves, playing on hit after hit.

Streaming tucks the credits away where nobody stumbles into them. Whose name kept turning up for you once you started reading the fine print?

comments.author: documentary_now
comments.body: There's a whole documentary about the Funk Brothers called Standing in the Shadows of Motown, and another one simply called The Wrecking Crew. Both will send you back to relisten to everything you thought you knew.

replies.author: vinyl_endgame
replies.body: saw the Motown one years ago and still think about it. these are the people who were actually in the room.

comments.author: reversecowbell
comments.body: Bass players get this worst. Carol Kaye played on so many sessions that people still argue about exactly which records. Nobody notices the bass until you take it out, and then the whole song falls over.

replies.author: b_side_believer
replies.body: the bass line is the ultimate deep cut. it's on every track and nobody ever requests it.

comments.author: SixStringBudget
comments.body: Guitar version: I spent ages trying to learn a riff note for note before finding out the recording was two session players with parts that interlock. No wonder I couldn't do it with one pair of hands.

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: this is why I'll argue the credits matter more than the cover art. the art tells you what the record wants to be. the credits tell you who actually made it.

late_comments.author: SixStringBudget
late_comments.body: Found this thread again and realized MMMBop got ruled defensible, so I still owe a real answer. The Macarena. I can also play it on guitar, which somehow makes it worse.

late_comments.author: vinyl_endgame
late_comments.body: Came across this while flipping through my copy of Rumours, so I tested my own side-two myth. The Chain opens side two, and the second slot is You Make Loving Fun, which was released as a single. The myth now survives on faith alone.
